study.title: Deuteronomy 27 The written law, the covenant proclaimed, and the curses against infidelity
study.overview: This chapter brings together a public act of renewing the covenant: the law should be recorded on stones, an altar should be erected without iron tool, and the people should hear blessings and curses before the LORD. The focus is not only to preserve information, but to form memory, worship, and obedience. The final section lists curses directed against sins that hurt fidelity to God and righteousness to others; the climax is the warning against not fully sustaining the words of the law. The chapter therefore shows that the alliance involves visible teaching, reverent worship and community moral responsibility.

outline.title: The law should be remembered and obeyed
outline.explanation: Moses, with the elders, and then with the priests of the Levites, command the people to keep all the commandments. Upon entering the earth, the words of the law should be written in stones plastered with lime, in a clear and permanent way. The altar of whole stones, without iron, points to worship ordained by God, and the sacrifices and meal before the LORD express joy of the covenant. The central message is that listening to the voice of God must result in concrete obedience.

outline.title: Blessing and curse before the tribes
outline.explanation: The tribes are distributed between Gerizim and Ebal to pronounce blessing and curse, while the Levites speak loudly. The people respond with "Amen," publicly assuming the terms of the covenant. The curses strike idolatry, dishonor parents, invasion of property limits, abuse of the weak and corruption of justice. The text shows that fidelity to God includes both correct worship and social righteousness.

outline.title: Hidden Sins and the Requirement of Comprehensive Obedience
outline.explanation: The list continues with forbidden sexual sins, hidden violence and bribery to kill innocents. The chapter ends with the curse on who does not confirm the words of this law to fulfill them. Thus unfaithfulness is not only public; the hidden is also before God. The closure reinforces that the alliance requires total submission, not a selective obedience.

study.context: The chapter is set on the eve of Israel's entry into the promised land. The text itself indicates that, after crossing the Jordan, there would be a solemn act involving written stones, an altar and the public proclamation of the words of the law. The notes indicate that the rite should take place near the Ebal and Gerizim mountains, with the people divided into two parts to listen and respond. There is not enough basis in the notes provided to state more than that about geography or exact date.
study.theology: Theologically, the chapter unites revelation, memory, worship and ethics. The law is not treated as something abstract: it is written, read, answered and assumed by the people. The altar of unwashed stones emphasizes that worship of the LORD must follow his own order, without human innovation that obscures his holiness. The curses show that God takes idolatry, family dishonor, injustice against vulnerable, sexual corruption and hidden violence seriously. The answer "Amen" indicates the agreement of the community with the justice of the covenant. The final verse teaches that the required obedience is integral; it is not enough to know the law, it must be confirmed in practice. In evangelical reading, this also points to the need for obedience that is not born of formalism, but from a heart subjected to God; yet, in the text itself, the main emphasis lies on Israel's pactual responsibility.

scholarViews.insight: The expression "all words of this law" may refer to the Deuteronomy set, but, considering the limited size of the surface of the stones, probably points more restricted to the Ten Commandments.

The writing of the law on the stones served to help the memory of the people, and the proclamation of blessings and curses aimed to move the affections, so that the law would not be treated as something indifferent.

The order to write the law clearly emphasizes that the monument should be durable and legible; the chapter, in its structure, presents the renewal of the covenant with blessings, curses and the final requirement to confirm all the words of the law.

questions: What changes when obedience ceases to be only something heard and becomes publicly assumed by the community?
What sins of this list show that biblical holiness involves both worship of God and righteousness with others?
In which areas of life do you tend to fulfill God's will in a partial way, instead of confirming "the words of this law" to fulfill them?
study.practice: Read this chapter as a call to visible and integral obedience. Take a break down time to review whether your faith is more in religious remembrance than in concrete practice. Confess to God any idolatry, injustice, family dishonor, indifference to the vulnerable or selective obedience. Then choose a specific action of fidelity for this week: repair an injustice, honor someone in the family, refuse dishonest advantage or return to a clear practice of biblical obedience.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not allow us to determine with certainty whether the "words of this law" in 27:3 cover the entire book of Deuteronomy or only the Ten Commandments; therefore, this question must remain open. There is also a textual divergence mentioned in the notes between Ebal and Gerizim in 27:4, but the biblical text provided follows Ebal. It is not safe to go beyond these observations based only on the material given.
